title: Malleus Maleficarum: Publication of the Hammer of Witches
description: Heinrich Kramer published the Malleus Maleficarum (Hammer of Witches) in 1487, the most influential demonological text of the witch-hunt period, going through at least 14 editions by 1520 and becoming a standard reference for prosecutors. The three-part work argued that witchcraft was real and primarily practiced by women (due to female moral weakness), provided a systematic theology of how witches operated through diabolical pact, and gave detailed procedural guidance for prosecution including interrogation and torture. Kramer had been expelled from Innsbruck by Bishop Golser in 1485 after conducting irregular proceedings, but the Malleus — with its appended papal bull — established his authority independently of local clerical opinion. The text's misogynistic framework linking female sexuality to diabolical susceptibility shaped prosecution patterns for two centuries.
historiographical_note: The Malleus's actual influence on prosecutions has been much debated. Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons situates it within the intellectual tradition of demonology, taking its theological arguments seriously. Christopher Mackay's modern critical edition restored Kramer as the sole author, contra earlier attributions to Sprenger. Lyndal Roper's work on the text's misogyny and its relationship to actual prosecution patterns is central to current gender-history approaches.
source_method: Kramer, Malleus Maleficarum (1487); Mackay critical edition (2006); secondary scholarship on demonology
